title: Semistable orbit closures and algebraic orbit dimensions
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field], $r\geq2$, and $G=\operatorname{PGL}_{r,k}$. Let $Z$ be a projective finite-type $k$-scheme [def-kun-projective, def-weil-finite-type-morphism] with a $G$-action and an ample $G$-linearized invertible module $A$, with semistable locus as in [lem-sfb-hilbert-plucker-pgl-linearization]. For every $z\in Z^{ss}(A)(k)$ the orbit $Gz$ is locally closed and
$$\dim(Gz)=\dim G-\dim G_z,$$
where $G_z$ is the scheme-theoretic stabilizer. Its closure inside $Z^{ss}(A)$ contains a unique orbit closed in $Z^{ss}(A)$. Every orbit contained in $\overline{Gz}\setminus Gz$ has strictly smaller dimension than $Gz$. The assertions hold also for nonreduced $Z$ and nonreduced stabilizers, with dimension the Krull dimension of the underlying schemes. The scheme, invertible-module, projective and ample conventions are [def-pc-scheme, def-sc-invertible-module, def-kun-projective, def-weil-pbc-ample-invertible-module]. The orbit is the image of the action map from G at z, and the stabilizer represents the group elements fixing z. Dimension is [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension].

source.place: Section 3.3, proof of Corollary 11(3), printed p.17, semistable orbit boundary with larger stabilizer. General orbit-dimension and unique closed orbit facts: Mumford--Fogarty--Kirwan, Geometric Invariant Theory, Chapter 1. Local references WANTED.

proof.text: First obtain a projective polarization in the embedding convention needed below. The projective-to-proper theorem makes $Z$ proper over $k$. The ample-to-very-ample immersion theorem, over $\operatorname{Spec}k$, gives $i:Z\to\mathbf P^n_k$ with $A^{\otimes d}\simeq i^*\mathcal O(1)$ for some $d>0$. Projective space is separated (it is proper by the same projective-to-proper theorem). The proper-to-separated-target theorem makes $i$ proper, so its image is closed. The immersion-with-closed-image theorem therefore makes $i$ a closed immersion. Thus the hypotheses of the projective-polarization section-algebra theorem apply to $(Z,A)$, including when $Z$ is nonreduced.

source.place: Tags 01VS/01VT (ample immersion), 01W6 (proper source to separated target), and schemes.tex Tag 01IQ (lemma-immersion-when-closed).

proof.text: Use the matrix model $G=D_+(\det)\subset\mathbf P(\operatorname{Mat}_r)$. Locally, a projective invertible matrix has a generator which is an invertible matrix; changing that generator multiplies it by a unit. Conversely invertible matrices modulo this scalar change glue to the same projective matrix. These inverse descriptions identify this open scheme with $\operatorname{PGL}_r$. The projective-polarization chart theorem applied to $\mathbf P^{r^2-1}$, $\mathcal O(1)$ and the degree-$r$ determinant makes $G$ affine of finite type. Its standard projective charts are polynomial rings localized at the nonzero determinant polynomial, hence reduced domains; their pairwise intersections are nonempty principal opens. Consequently $G$ is integral. The finite-type-over-Noetherian theorem makes $Z$ and $G$ Noetherian (a field is Noetherian). The minimal-closed-subset theorem gives the descending-chain condition on their closed subsets: the members of an infinite strict descending chain would have no minimal member. The compact-subsets theorem then makes every subset quasi-compact. In particular their open subschemes have finite affine covers and remain finite type over $k$.

source.place: Chapter 5, Example 5.49 (PGL quotient); explicit projective matrix charts. Auxiliary Stacks Tags 0EKE (affine polarization chart), 01T6, 04ZA. Also Tag 01OZ (properties.tex, lemma-Noetherian-topology).

proof.text: We will use rational-point detection as follows. In a nonempty locally closed subscheme of a finite-type $k$-scheme, choose a nonempty affine open $V$. It is quasi-compact and $T_0$, so the closed-point theorem gives a closed point of $V$. The closed-point residue-field theorem makes it $k$-rational. Thus every such nonempty locally closed subset has a $k$-point. In particular $k$-points are dense: if the complement of their closure were nonempty, apply this argument to that open complement. A nonempty fibre over a rational point also has a rational point, since it is finite type over $k$.

Fix $z\in Z^{ss}(k)$ and write $a_z:G\to Z$, $g\mapsto gz$, and $O=a_z(|G|)$. Over affine charts the coordinate map is finite type because generators over $k$ also generate over the target algebra; quasi-compact inverse images are supplied by Step 2. Thus $a_z$ and its fibres over rational points are finite type. Its image is constructible: over each affine open $W\subset Z$, the inverse image has a finite affine cover by Step 2, and each chart maps to the affine finite-type scheme $W$. Apply the affine Chevalley theorem to each of these finitely many maps and take their union; this gives constructibility on every member of a finite affine cover of $Z$. Let $C=\overline O$ in $Z$, with the reduced induced closed subscheme structure. It is finite type, since its affine coordinate rings are quotients of those of $Z$. It is irreducible: a cover of $C$ by two closed subsets pulls back to a cover of the irreducible $G$, so one contains $O$, hence all of $C$. For each $g\in G(k)$, the identity $g a_z(h)=a_z(gh)$ shows $gO=O$ and therefore $gC=C$.

source.place: Proposition 1.65(b), printed p.27; constructible-image argument. Reduced induced structure: Stacks Tag 01J3 (schemes.tex, lemma-reduced-closed-subscheme).

proof.text: Choose a nonempty affine open $W\subset C$. The constructible set $O\cap W$ is dense in $W$, so the constructible-open theorem supplies a nonempty open $V\subset C$ contained in $O$. Choose $v\in V(k)$ by Step 3; its fibre under $a_z$ is nonempty, so Step 3 also gives $h\in G(k)$ with $hz=v$. Put $T=\bigcup_{g\in G(k)}gV$, an open subset of $C$ contained in $O$. It contains all rational points of $O$: any such point lifts to $G(k)$ by the same fibre argument, and hence is a translate of $v$. The closed subset $a_z^{-1}(C\setminus T)$ of $G$ has no rational point; Step 3 makes it empty. Thus $O=T$ is open in its closure, proving local closedness. This argument applies to every rational point of $Z$, without using semistability.

source.place: Proposition 1.65(b), printed p.27, translate-cover argument, with the rational-point detection of Step 3 made explicit.

proof.text: The scheme-theoretic stabilizer $H=G_z$ is the fibre $a_z^{-1}(z)$: for every $k$-algebra $R$ its points are exactly those $h\in G(R)$ with $hz_R=z_R$. Since $Z$ is separated, this equalizer with the constant map is a closed subscheme of $G$: it is the pullback of the closed diagonal of $Z$ along $g\mapsto(gz,z)$, and the closed-immersion base-change theorem makes it closed. It is a subgroup by $hz=z$, $h'z=z\Rightarrow hh'z=z$ and $hz=z\Rightarrow h^{-1}z=z$. In particular $H$ is finite type. For $g\in G(k)$, left multiplication by $g$ gives an isomorphism $H\simeq a_z^{-1}(gz)$, with inverse left multiplication by $g^{-1}$: over every $R$, $(gh)z=gz$ if and only if $hz=z$. This identifies the fibre schemes, including all nilpotents.

source.place: Chapter 1, group actions, orbit map on printed p.27; fibre translation checked on all algebra-valued points.

proof.text: Apply the irreducible fibre-dimension theorem to $a_z:G\to Z$. Both schemes are finite type, and $G$ is nonempty irreducible. It gives $n\ge0$ with $\dim G=\dim C+n$ and a nonempty dense open of $G$ where the local topological fibre dimension is $n$. Choose a rational $g$ in this open by Step 3. By Step 6 its fibre at $gz$ is $gH$, with $g$ corresponding to the identity of $H$. The rational-point stalk/topological-dimension comparison identifies this local fibre dimension with $\dim\mathcal O_{H,e}$. The group-identity dimension theorem gives $\dim\mathcal O_{H,e}=\dim H$, without smoothness or reducedness of $H$. Finally $O$ is a nonempty open in the irreducible locally finite-type $C$, so the open-dimension theorem gives $\dim O=\dim C$. Finite-type dimensions are finite. Consequently $\dim(Gz)=\dim G-\dim G_z$ as an equality of finite integers.

source.place: Tag 0B2L (lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic), (2)(a),(b); Tag 0A21 (lemma-dimension-locally-algebraic), (3). groupoids.tex Tag 045X (lemma-group-scheme-finite-type-field) and algebra.tex Tag 00OU supply the stabilizer comparison.

proof.text: Put $S=Z^{ss}(A)$ and $C_S=C\cap S$. By definition $S$ is the union of the nonvanishing opens of positive-degree invariant sections of powers of $A$. The linearization makes each such open invariant, so $O\subset S$, and likewise $Gy\subset S$ for every $y\in S(k)$. Thus $C_S$ is the closure of $O$ in $S$, is irreducible, and $O$ is open in $C$ (Step 5) and in $C_S$. Set $B=C\setminus O$, the boundary of $O$ in its closure in $Z$; its part $B\cap S=C_S\setminus O$ is the boundary inside $S$. $B$ is closed in $C$, proper, and stable under $G(k)$. For $y\in B(k)$, $a_y^{-1}(C)$ is closed in $G$ and contains $G(k)$, as $gC=C$; density from Step 3 makes it all of $G$. Since $O$ is open in $C$, $a_y^{-1}(B)=G\setminus a_y^{-1}(O)$ is closed in $G$, and it contains $G(k)$ as $gB=B$; so it is all of $G$ and $Gy\subset B$. For any chain of irreducible closed subsets of $B$ (closed in $C$, as $B$ is), adjoining the irreducible $C$ adds a strict step. Therefore $\dim B<\dim C$ when $B$ is nonempty, and $\dim C=\dim O$ by Step 7. Since $O\subset C_S\subset C$, subspace monotonicity also gives $\dim C_S=\dim O$. Consequently every orbit in $\overline{Gz}\setminus Gz$, with the closure taken in $Z$ or in $S$, has dimension at most $\dim B<\dim O$. Subspace monotonicity here follows directly by taking closures of a chain in the larger space: their intersections with the original subspace recover the original chain, so all inclusions remain strict.

source.place: Proposition 1.66 (Orbit Lemma), printed pp.27--28; explicit chain argument for the boundary dimension drop. Semistability is the convention in the item.

proof.text: The set of dimensions of orbits of rational points of $C_S$ is a nonempty set of nonnegative integers (it contains $\dim O$). Choose $y\in C_S(k)$ whose orbit has least dimension. If $Gy$ were not closed in $S$, its boundary in its closure in $S$ would be a nonempty locally closed subset of a finite-type scheme and hence would contain $w\in S(k)$ by Step 3. Its closure lies in the closed subset $C_S\subset S$, so $w\in C_S$. Applying Step 8 with $y$ in place of $z$ gives $\dim Gw<\dim Gy$, contradicting minimality. Thus $C_S$ contains an orbit closed in $S$.

source.place: Proposition 1.66, printed pp.27--28, minimum-dimension orbit proof, applied inside the invariant closure $C_S$.

proof.text: For uniqueness suppose $O_1=Gy_1$ and $O_2=Gy_2$ are distinct orbits in $C_S$ closed in $S$. Semistability gives invariant sections $s_i\in H^0(Z,A^{\otimes d_i})$, $d_i>0$, nonzero at $y_i$. Replace them by $s_1^{d_2}$ and $s_2^{d_1}$ to give both degree $d_1d_2$. At each of the two rational points the equation $s_1^{d_2}+c s_2^{d_1}=0$ excludes at most one $c\in k$, since the relevant one of these sections is nonzero. An algebraically closed field is infinite: if it were finite, $1+\prod_{a\in k}(T-a)$ would have no root. Choose $c$ avoiding both exceptions and put $s=s_1^{d_2}+c s_2^{d_1}$. Then $U=Z_s$ is an invariant affine finite-type open by Step 1 and the polarization chart theorem, and it contains $y_1,y_2$. It also contains $z$: otherwise the invariant closed zero set of $s$ would contain $O$ and $C$, contradicting $y_1\in C\cap U$. Invariance then gives $O\subset U$.

source.place: Tag 0EKE (lemma-proper-ample-delete-affine), affine charts as packaged in the polarization node. Common section is an explicit elementary linear combination.

proof.text: Write $U=\operatorname{Spec}E$. Each $O_i$ is closed in $U$, because it is closed in $S$ and $U\subset S$. Give it the reduced induced closed structure $Y_i=\operatorname{Spec}(E/I_i)$, with $I_i$ radical. Distinct orbits have disjoint rational points. If $Y_1\cap Y_2$ were nonempty, Step 3 would give a rational point in it. Its two nonempty orbit-map fibres would have rational points, making $y_1$ and $y_2$ translates of one another, a contradiction. Thus $Y_1\cap Y_2=\varnothing$, whence $I_1+I_2=E$: a proper sum would lie in a maximal ideal and give a point in the intersection. The Chinese remainder theorem now makes $E\to E/I_1\times E/I_2$ surjective.

The quotient in Step 11 is equivariant for the full group scheme. Indeed $G$ and $Y_i$ are reduced affine finite-type schemes over the algebraically closed $k$, so their product is reduced by the reduced-product theorem. For $b\in I_i$, pull back $b$ along $G\times Y_i\to U$. Its value at every pair $(g,y)\in G(k)\times Y_i(k)$ is $b(gy)=0$, because $O_i$ is an orbit. The product vanishing principle therefore makes this pulled-back function zero. In coordinates the composite $E\to E\otimes_k k[G]\to (E/I_i)\otimes_k k[G]$ kills $I_i$, which is exactly the condition for the coaction to descend. The coactions consequently descend to each $E/I_i$ and to their product; the quotient map is equivariant. This argument does not require $E$ reduced.

source.place: Group action stability, printed pp.26--27; affine verification using the existing product vanishing principle (blueprint lem-wf-affine-product-reduced).

proof.text: In $F=E/I_1\times E/I_2$, the element $b=(0,1)$ is invariant: the action preserves each of the two factors and their scalar constants. Apply the PGL geometric-reductivity power-lifting statement to the surjective equivariant map $E\twoheadrightarrow F$. Both are finitely generated $k$-algebras (a finite product of the two quotients is generated by their generators and $(1,0)$). It gives $N>0$ and $f\in E^G$ mapping to $b^N=b$. Thus $f$ is zero on $Y_1$ and one on $Y_2$. Only the lifting of a power is used; exactness of taking invariants is not assumed.

source.place: Introduction, printed p.2, geometric reductivity as lifting powers of invariant functions; Sections 9.1--9.2 and Theorem 9.7.6. Read online at https://arxiv.org/pdf/1005.2398; local PDF WANTED.

proof.text: Set $a=f(z)\in k$. Invariance says that the pullback of $f$ along the orbit map $a_z:G\to U$ is the constant $a$: restrict the coaction identity $\rho(f)=f\otimes1$ at $z$. Hence $O$ lies in the closed zero set $V(f-a)$ in $U$. Its closure in $U$ is $C\cap U$, so both $y_1,y_2$ lie in that zero set. Evaluation at $y_1$ gives $a=0$, and evaluation at $y_2$ gives $a=1$, a contradiction. Thus the closed orbit from Step 9 is unique.

source.place: Agent affine separation argument using the power-lifting property in the introduction, printed p.2; no adequate-moduli-space existence theorem is invoked.

proof.text: Every construction above used only the underlying topology of $Z$ for orbit closures and dimensions, but used the actual scheme fibres in Step 6. The stabilizer in Step 7 was never replaced by its reduced subgroup: its identity local-ring dimension equals its full scheme dimension by the cited group theorem even when it is nonreduced. In Step 12 reduced structures were put only on the two closed orbit subsets to test invariance of their ideals; the ambient algebra $E$ and the geometric-reductivity map were allowed to be nonreduced. Consequently all conclusions proved above hold for nonreduced $Z$ and nonreduced stabilizers, as stated.
